rationale: Direct upper-midsize (E-segment) rival of the 5 Series in Germany and the UK with the same powertrain mix (48V mild-hybrid petrol/diesel, petrol and diesel PHEV); ADAC names the BMW 5er Touring as a direct competitor and German press runs the E 220 d against the 520d head to head.

statement: Reviewer states the optional air suspension with adaptive dampers gives a balance of ride comfort, safety and dynamics unique in the class and makes long motorway stages stress-free; only short sharp impacts (manhole covers) come through, worsened by the 20-inch tyres.

Reviewer states driving stability and agility surpass the already excellent predecessor; the car passes the ADAC evasion test easily and combines composure with agility like no other car in the class.

Reviewer states the standard steering is direct (2.3 turns lock to lock), precise and gives good feedback, among the best in the class; rear-axle steering is offered for the saloon but not the estate (except E 53 AMG).
Reviewer states the brake pedal feels doughy with an undefined pressure point, making precise, smooth stopping a real challenge (although the measured 31.0 m from 100 km/h is sports-car level).
quote: Zu teigig fühlt sich das Bremspedal bei Betätigung an

statement: Reviewer strongly criticises the touch surfaces on the steering wheel as impractical to frustrating; mis-operation happens daily and is hard to avoid even after long familiarisation.
Reviewer states the small touch slider for volume below the central screen does not allow precise adjustment and puts the small volume roller of earlier models at the top of the wish list.

Reviewer states there are no dedicated keys for main functions such as navigation or phone, so one must go through the main menu; a few quality physical keys like the predecessor's would have been worthwhile, and dropping them saves cost but worsens usability.

Reviewer praises the 14.4-inch central display for high resolution, fast responses, fluid animations and mostly large enough touch areas, plus a sharp, easily readable 12.3-inch digital instrument display.
Reviewer states the low-mounted central display makes the augmented-reality camera view of the road ahead of little use, because looking down at it distracts more than a higher-placed screen would.
Reviewer states voice control works first-class and for the first time can be used without the wake word 'Hey Mercedes'.

Reviewer states the climate controls, fixed at the bottom of the touchscreen, are clearly more cumbersome than a separate climate panel: temperature requires first touching the number and then using plus/minus; the air-volume thumbwheels are unlit.
Reviewer states there is neither a button nor a touch field in the climate menu for the heated steering wheel, leaving only voice control to switch it independently of the seat heating.

Reviewer calls the flush, automatically extending door handles a constant annoyance: the mechanism is partly stubborn and sticks, and in many everyday situations the handles do not extend and must be pressed firmly.
Reviewer criticises the mirror adjustment in the driver's door, now a touch-sensitive plate that must be pressed in exactly the right spot, which often needs a careful look away from the road.
Reviewer states wide roof pillars, non-retractable rear headrests and the narrow, high rear window considerably restrict the view to the rear, and the body ends are hard to judge.

Reviewer rates the 'Digital Light' LED headlights with dynamic high-beam assist as among the best currently available for the money, with very bright, even illumination; only a headlight washer is missing.

Reviewer states the estate's boot is among the largest (505 l to the cover, 1,570 l max measured), with a very low 60 cm sill flush with the floor, standard power tailgate and an auto-retracting load cover; only the folded seats leave a small step.
Reviewer states rear legroom suffices for passengers up to 2.10 m with the front seat set for 1.85 m, and headroom is generous; two sit comfortably but three adults are tight.
Reviewer states the sense of space in front is only impaired by the bulky centre console and the dark headliner of AMG Line models.
Reviewer states the inductive smartphone charging tray is comparatively small and hard to access.
Reviewer states the electric parking brake button sits low left under the steering wheel and is very hard for the front passenger to reach.
Reviewer states the car is well built with tight, even panel gaps, and the interior looks very noble with materials that feel high quality, helped by extensive leather on doors and dashboard.

Reviewer states several details do not match the price level: plain plastic sun visors, fragile-feeling stalks, an unlined glovebox lid, a soft door-pull and creaking when the dashboard is grabbed firmly.
Reviewer states the cabin is remarkably quiet (64.6 dB(A) at 130 km/h) with little suspension or wind noise; only the gruff four-cylinder diesel note clouds the refinement.

Reviewer states the 2.0 diesel mild hybrid responds well thanks to the e-motor at low revs but does not quite reach the rev-happiness of the BMW counterpart with two-stage turbocharging, and feels somewhat sluggish versus a six-cylinder.
quote: an die Drehfreude etwa des BMW-Pendants mit Stufenaufladung

statement: Reviewer praises the standard nine-speed automatic for smooth shifts, fitting shift points, quick multi-gear kickdowns and comfortable creeping when manoeuvring (sub-grade 1.0).
Reviewer states consumption of 5.8 l/100 km in the ADAC Ecotest is pleasingly low for the size, giving about 1,135 km per tank now that the larger 66-litre tank is standard.
Reviewer states the Burmester surround system with 21 speakers, Dolby Atmos and 4D seat-transducer sound, standard from AMG Line Premium, sounds very good.
Reviewer notes wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto are standard, with up to six USB-C ports (four front, two rear) plus inductive charging.
Reviewer states the range of driver assistance systems is very extensive, but many safety systems cost extra, which it calls incomprehensible for a car costing over 80,000 euros.
Reviewer calls the car extremely expensive: the tested AMG Line Premium 4MATIC starts at 81,313 euros, the test car came to just under 100,000 euros, and only a two-year warranty is given.
Reviewer states the optional fully electric multicontour seats with massage, memory, four-way lumbar, extendable thigh support and adjustable bolsters give good overall seat comfort.
Reviewer states the front centre armrest is hard at its front end and the thinly padded door armrest makes the elbow hurt on longer drives.
Reviewer highlights a high safety level: five Euro NCAP stars with 92 % for adult occupants, plus Pre-Safe Impulse Side and height-adjustable rear outer belts.
Reviewer states the 4.95 m length, 2.08 m width and 12 m turning circle make the estate rather unsuited to city traffic, where parking becomes a test of patience.
Reviewer ranks the E 220 d 4Matic T-Modell first with 3,322 of 5,000 points, narrowly ahead of the BMW 520d xDrive Touring (3,294).
Reviewer states the air suspension gives a soft ride with high load reserves and very calm motorway running that the BMW 5 Series Touring cannot match.
Reviewer calls the E-Class the most engaging of the three, with precise steering, good feedback and strong limit handling, while the BMW pushes wide earlier and lacks front-axle bite.
Reviewer praises the E 220 d's economy: 6.0 l/100 km on test versus 6.2 l for the 520d xDrive Touring (WLTP 5.0 vs 5.7 l).
Reviewer states the diesel pulls with strong low-end torque (440 Nm) so that it feels like a three-litre diesel.
Reviewer states the E 220 d is slower to 100 km/h than the 520d xDrive Touring (8.4 s vs 7.8 s) and lacks eagerness at the top of the rev range.
Reviewer states the glass of the cockpit displays does not sit cleanly and rates the BMW's build quality and body structure higher.
Reviewer states the E-Class relies on touch operation of its two screens and lacks a rotary controller; it prefers the BMW's rotary-push controller, especially while driving.
Reviewer states the lane-keeping and lane-change assistants do not always work reliably and intervene suddenly, more disruptive than helpful, a criticism it applies equally to the BMW.
Reviewer states the E-Class T-Modell is noticeably airier in the rear than the BMW 5 Series Touring, whose rear knee room is the tightest of the three despite its greater length.
Reviewer states the E-Class has the largest boot in the test (615-1,830 l versus 570-1,700 l for the BMW) plus a larger underfloor compartment.
Reviewer states the multicontour seats offer long-distance comfort but feel narrow at the shoulders, while it calls the BMW's optional comfort seats first-class.
Reviewer praises the E-Class for a soothing calm in the noise measurements, better than the BMW.
Reviewer calls the E-Class the most expensive car in the test (base 69,556 euros, test car 82,009 euros vs 64,350 / 75,930 euros for the BMW) and scores it lower on costs.
Owner (E 200 estate) states the cabin is quiet and the car is well suited to long motorway trips.

vfc_level2: Driver assistance, automated driving, overall technology
statement: Owner praises the driver assistance: adaptive cruise, semi-autonomous steering for 20-30 seconds, automatic braking and camera/radar aids that help in fog.
Owner likes the navigation based on Google Maps.
Owner reports fuel use of about 7.0-7.1 l/100 km on a mixed route with the E 200 petrol estate.
Owner (E 400 e plug-in hybrid saloon) states the engine is noticeably noisy and buzzy at low revs, louder than comparable BMW or Audi diesels, and recommends driving electrically where possible.
Owner reports a creaking/scraping noise when lifting off the throttle, also at idle; the dealer suspects the turbo wastegate valve but the owner is not convinced.

Owner (E 220 d saloon, under 1.90 m) states the front headrests cannot be raised or moved back and press on the neck, causing neck and shoulder pain on long drives; the dealer only offers a modification that would void the warranty, and the owner rates the W213 far better.

Owner (review text describes the E 300 de diesel plug-in hybrid) states that under firm acceleration in electric mode the drive briefly disconnects before the combustion engine and then the e-motor join in.
Owner (E 220 d saloon) reports about 5.9 l/100 km on average and over 1,400 km on one tank at up to 140 km/h.
Owner states the car is very quiet.
Owner reports no faults after about six months and over 30,000 km.
Owner (E 220 d saloon) reports the flush door handles did not extend, so the car could not be opened with the key fob or phone and a spare key was needed.
Owner reports a gearbox fault warning before a service visit, which had cleared by the time the technician arrived.
Owner (E 220 d saloon) describes the car as very comfortable.
Owner reports economical running at about 5 l/100 km at 130 km/h on the motorway.
Owner states the voice assistant talks too much and interrupts.
Owner (E 200 petrol saloon) reports 14 visits to the service centre, without further detail.

Forum user (1.86 m, ownership not stated) reports hitting the left knee on the door armrest and the right knee on the centre-console protrusion, and finds the cabin cramped compared with earlier E-Class and C-Class models.
Forum user criticises the W214's interior materials as poor.
Second forum user (ownership not stated) reports the same right-knee contact with the centre-console area of the W214.
Third forum user (ownership not stated) reports the same knee issue, finds the console edge uncomfortable to rest a leg against and says the cabin does not feel roomy.
Forum user who says they have used the new E-Class states the interior material quality is well ahead of the previous model.
Forum user praises MBUX as more intuitive and customisable than before.
Forum user states rear-seat space could be larger and that the BMW 5 Series feels roomier overall.

rationale: Mercedes' electric E-segment saloon and the direct rival of the BMW i5 in Germany and the UK; AUTO BILD tests the EQE 350 head to head against the i5 eDrive40 at near-identical base prices (70,995 vs 70,200 EUR).

statement: Reviewer states the optional Airmatic air suspension gives very good overall ride comfort, excellent at medium and high speeds, though response to urban bumps could be better on the 20-inch tyres.
Reviewer states the cabin is exceptionally quiet with the optional acoustic glazing (63.3 dB(A) at 130 km/h) and the encapsulated e-drive is practically inaudible even under load or recuperation.
Reviewer states the EQE 350+ achieved about 530 km in the ADAC Ecotest (20.0 kWh/100 km incl. charging losses), a really good value that should still leave around 400 km in winter.
Reviewer states DC charging (peak 171 kW, 145 kW average, 10-80 % in about 30 minutes) cannot keep up with the best EVs, and there is no heat pump.

Reviewer praises the standard navigation's charging-stop planning with automatic battery preconditioning, selectable arrival charge levels and an eco charging mode, calling the energy management well thought out and easy to use.
Reviewer calls the charging-port cover with an additional rubber cap outdated and unworthy of the price, noting Mercedes has more elegant solutions on other EQ models.
Reviewer rates stability as first-class and says the optional 10-degree rear-axle steering makes the almost five-metre saloon feel nearly as handy as a compact car, with a 10.6 m turning circle.
Reviewer states the steering feels solid but somewhat decoupled, and with rear-axle steering it is never quite clear at pace how much the rear wheels steer, which hurts precision.

Reviewer criticises the brake pedal as very doughy with a pressure point that wanders with speed, making braking hard to modulate; Mercedes should urgently fix this (stopping distance of 33.8 m is good).

Reviewer states the 292 PS rear motor accelerates surprisingly briskly despite the weight (60-100 km/h in 3.4 s), delivers power smoothly without vibration, and the adaptive recuperation via paddles or Eco Assist is well tuned.
Reviewer states the steering wheel's 18 touch surfaces often react unreliably and give no haptic feedback, so the driver must glance to check each command, causing distraction.

Reviewer painfully misses a classic rotary volume knob and direct-select keys for main functions (navigation, radio, phone); the alternative touch strip below the screen feels cheap and is only moderately usable.
Reviewer states the immense function range and partly nested menus force the driver to look away from the road much longer than intended, and the low screen position adds distraction.
Reviewer rates the graphics and touch response of the standard 11.9-inch central display as first-class, with pleasantly large touch areas and a clearly readable digital instrument cluster.
Reviewer states the flush door handles (with Keyless Go) do not always extend reliably as the key approaches, and opening forces are very high when the car fails to detect the intent to open.

Reviewer states the body ends cannot be seen from the driver's seat and the all-round visibility measurement is poor: A-pillars reach far forward, and bulky fixed rear headrests and a small rear window limit the rear view.
Reviewer rates the optional Digital Light headlights (over 1.3 million micro-mirrors, road projections) as among the best available, with excellent illumination; a headlight washer is missing.
Reviewer states the saloon boot holds only 380 l (less than the combustion E-Class), the boot-lid opening is small for bulky items, and the 77 cm sill with an 18 cm step down makes loading tiresome.
Reviewer notes that, unlike other EVs, the EQE has no front trunk, so charging cables go in a small underfloor box that is hard to reach when the boot is loaded; a frunk would be the better solution.
Reviewer states rear legroom is opulent but headroom suits only passengers up to about 1.85 m, and the high floor with a low bench gives a sharp knee angle that becomes uncomfortable.
Reviewer calls the 750 kg maximum towing capacity meagre for a car of this size and power class.

Reviewer sees cost-cutting at odds with the price: unpadded sun visors, hard plastic on the lower front door panels (foamed on the E-Class), sharp edges at the wireless-charging slot, a creaking armrest and unlined door bins.
Reviewer states the interior looks noble, materials largely feel high quality and the highly configurable ambient lighting creates a lounge atmosphere at night.
Reviewer criticises the vents above the central display, where airflow intensity cannot be set independently of airflow direction.

Reviewer criticises buyer-unfriendly pricing: adaptive cruise and even an auto-dimming mirror cost extra on a 70,000-euro car, many options are tied to expensive packages (a head-up display effectively needs almost 30,000 euros of packages) and the test car exceeded 100,000 euros.

Reviewer states even the standard front seats offer extensive electric adjustment with four-way lumbar, and the optional multicontour seats add memory, extendable cushion and massage, giving very comfortable support (side support only satisfactory).

Reviewer states rear seat comfort falls clearly short of the front, the rear middle seat is too narrow for adults, and the hard upper door armrest and unpadded front of the centre armrest spoil the driving position.
Reviewer states the electric parking brake button left of the steering wheel can hardly be reached by the passenger in an emergency.
Reviewer ranks the EQE 350 second with 612 of 800 points behind the BMW i5 eDrive40 (635), mainly on handling, braking, boot space and price.
Reviewer measured 404 km range for the EQE 350 versus 383 km for the i5 eDrive40.
Reviewer states the EQE charges at up to 170 kW (10-80 % in 32 min) versus 205 kW (30 min) for the i5, and uses slightly more energy on the economy loop.
Reviewer finds the EQE's drive refined and responsive, but the i5 eDrive40 is faster in the acceleration tests and livelier.

Reviewer describes the EQE as comfort-oriented and handy thanks to the optional rear-axle steering, but its steering needs getting used to, while the i5 is lighter, more playful and steers more precisely.
Reviewer measured 33.2 m from 100 km/h with warm brakes for the EQE versus 32.3 m for the i5.
Reviewer describes the EQE's optional air suspension (2,083 EUR) as very comfortable and smooth.
Reviewer praises the EQE's bright, well-structured displays and menus and rates its voice control among the fastest.
Reviewer describes the EQE interior as more opulent, with high-quality build.
Reviewer states the EQE's front seats are narrower with less shoulder support and the seat adjustment gives no feedback, rating the i5 better here.
Reviewer states the EQE offers more rear legroom than the i5, though slightly less rear headroom and width.
Reviewer states the EQE's boot holds 430 l and payload is 475 kg, versus 490 l and 578 kg for the i5.
Reviewer measured the EQE quieter than the i5: 61 dB(A) versus 63 dB(A) at 130 km/h.
Reviewer notes the EQE test car cost over 10,000 euros more than the i5 test car (93,123 vs 82,680 EUR) and rates the BMW better on value.
Owner (EQE 350 saloon) states the ride is very comfortable and absorbs bumps well.
Owner rates the EQE's quietness above their previous Peugeot 508s and Kia Sorento.
Owner praises the standard audio system as better than in their previous cars.
Owner reports over 500 km of range in summer with average consumption of about 18 kWh/100 km.
Owner (EQE 300 saloon) states comfort is far better than in their previous Tesla Model 3 Long Range.

Owner, initially worried about rear-wheel drive, reports that on snow and ice in the mountains the stability systems quickly brought the car back in line when they deliberately provoked a slide, unlike their previous Tesla.
Owner (EQE 350 saloon) states the motor has enough power for daily driving in all conditions.
Owner (company car, new since November 2024) states they are very happy with the EQE and finds much of the online criticism unfounded.
Owner states the rear-wheel steering makes the car very manoeuvrable and recommends ordering it.
Owner (EQE 300, built 11/2023) calls the front camera valuable because the view ahead over the bonnet is almost nil, and says the rear camera works well.
Owner states the 360-degree camera greys out exactly the area closest to the car, which would be the most useful.
Owner states they use the traffic-light camera view daily.
Owner states the optional Burmester sound system is better than the standard one.
Owner states the Digital Light projector headlights are worth having.
Owner states the standard comfort suspension is excellent and air suspension is not needed.
Owner states the boot is smaller than expected: a golf bag requires folding a rear seat section, and two golf bags the whole bench.
Owner wishes they had 22 kW AC charging; their car has 11 kW because 22 kW was an extra-cost option.
Owner wishes for front seat ventilation.
Owner notes the upholstery is faux leather and wishes for genuine leather.
Owner says they love the car and find the design beautiful despite online criticism.
Owner (EQE 300, about one month and 3,500 km) reports more interior creaks and rattles than expected for Mercedes' quality standard, otherwise no failures.
Owner finds acceleration good up to 120 km/h but sluggish above that despite 245 PS, attributing it to the S-Class-like weight.

Forum user states the EQE has noticeably more interior space than the EQA or EQB.
Forum user states charging power could be higher: the 400-volt architecture is mature and reliable but not fast.
Owner (EQE 350+, bought used with 5,000 km, four weeks of ownership, switched from an Ioniq 5) describes the ride as like a flying carpet and does not regret the switch.

rationale: Audi's new combustion/PHEV E-segment model (originally planned as the A7) and the direct rival of the 520i/520d/530e in Germany; ADAC names the BMW 5er Touring as its first competitor.

statement: Reviewer states the optional adaptive air suspension (2,150 EUR) gives very good ride comfort with the right tuning for every situation, calling it money well spent, though 20-inch wheels are not fully masked over deep manhole covers.

Reviewer states the A6 Avant with optional rear-axle steering passes the ADAC evasion test with excellent stability, feels agile for a 2.1-tonne estate and is manoeuvrable with an 11.6 m turning circle.
Reviewer states the steering feels somewhat decoupled and synthetic in typical Audi fashion, withholding information about grip, and self-centres conspicuously eagerly in town.
Reviewer rates the 32.5 m stop from 100 km/h as excellent and finds the integrated brake system responsive and easy to modulate, with a crisp, short pedal.
Reviewer states the 2.0 TDI quattro needs only 5.7 l/100 km in the ADAC measurement and breaks the 1,000 km range barrier with its 60-litre tank.
Reviewer states the MHEV plus system makes the drivetrain respond quickly with harmonious power delivery and allows electric creeping, though the e-motor stops assisting above 140 km/h.
Reviewer states the diesel is clearly audible when warming up, with slight steering-wheel vibrations, and always sounds rougher than a comparable petrol engine.

Reviewer states the 7-speed S tronic dual-clutch usually picks the right gear, is intuitive to operate via the small slider, and pulls away and manoeuvres smoothly, now with hardly any jerk when the e-motor couples.

Reviewer states the C9 no longer reaches its predecessor's finesse: hard plastic on the lower rear door panels, sun visors without fabric, a piano-black console trim that attracts dust and fingerprints, and creaks when resting a hand on the trim.
Reviewer criticises that on the base car or with only the Tech package a plain black blank panel, a placeholder for the optional passenger display, dominates the right side of the dashboard.

Reviewer states climate control runs entirely through the central display: key functions are always visible, but the touch fields are small, cannot be found by feel, and air distribution requires opening a submenu.
Reviewer notes the vent thumbwheels let airflow intensity be set independently of direction, front and rear centre.
Reviewer states the remaining touch keys on the steering wheel work in a jerky and only conditionally reliable way, even though model year 2026 brought back rollers.
Reviewer welcomes that from model year 2026 classic thumb rollers for the trip computer and volume replace the swipe fields on the steering wheel, improving operation.
Reviewer criticises that Audi moved the light controls, mirror adjustment and central locking into a touch panel in the door, which works as jerkily and unreliably as the steering-wheel touch keys.
Reviewer welcomes that a haptic rotary volume control remains in the centre console and that driver-assistance and parking functions each keep a small physical button.

Reviewer praises the standard OLED panorama display as sharp and high-contrast; the central screen is curved toward the driver so even its right edge is reachable, and the trim below supports the hand.
Reviewer praises the infotainment search function, which finds settings and functions and cleverly integrates the owner's manual, putting Audi far ahead of many Chinese brands here.

Reviewer states the digital instrument cluster, despite MY2026 graphics upgrades (not retrofittable to earlier cars), does not match the excellent readability of the predecessor, and detail fonts are partly too small.
Reviewer praises how easily the speed-limit warning (via a steering-wheel favourite key) and the lane-keeping assist (one long press on the indicator stalk) can be switched off.
Reviewer states the optional lane-centring with route-based speed adaptation (Tech Plus package) works reliably in everyday testing and is a real relief on long trips.

Reviewer states useful systems such as blind-spot warning, exit warning and rear cross-traffic braking cost extra and are tied to partly expensive packages; steering-wheel and rear seat heating come only in the 7,510-euro Tech pro package.
Reviewer states the 64,550-euro base price sits mid-field among competitors and that, smartly equipped (e.g. the 2,480-euro Tech package), the value for money is right.
Reviewer states the 475 l boot is below average among competitors and has no large underfloor storage, though the low 66 cm sill and suitable opening make it easy to use.
Reviewer praises the standard foot-kick tailgate opening, which in the dark projects a symbol under the rear showing where to kick, plus separate buttons to close only or close and lock.

Reviewer states the rear offers noticeably less space than the predecessor, although legroom still suits passengers over 2 m and headroom up to 1.95 m; the high beltline and C-pillar beside the head reduce the sense of space.
Reviewer regrets that the new A6 replaces the easy-to-use bar door handles with recessed grips with an internal button, and notes such grips can hamper rescue after an accident.
Reviewer states the doors have only two detent positions, which makes getting out in tight spaces harder, and with the door fully open one must lean far out to reach the pull handle.
Reviewer notes the car can optionally be locked, unlocked and started via smartphone or smartwatch without taking the phone out, and digital keys can be shared with other users via the Audi app.

Reviewer highlights the optional individual contour seats as offering the best seat comfort, with adjustable cushion and backrest bolsters (a rarity), massage, ventilation, four-way lumbar and memory.
Reviewer states the standard seats are fairly basic, with only height, fore-aft and backrest angle adjustable manually.
Reviewer notes Apple CarPlay and Android Auto work with and without cable as standard, with inductive charging and USB-C front and rear also standard.
Reviewer states even the standard Audi sound system with ten speakers, centre speaker and subwoofer is remarkably good.
Reviewer rates the Matrix LED headlights (Tech package) as very good with bright, even light and a reliable glare-free high beam; a headlight washer is available at extra cost.
Reviewer states the all-round visibility result is only passable because of the wide D-pillars and rear headrests that cannot be lowered, and the front edge of the long bonnet is not visible.
Reviewer states the cabin is pleasantly quiet with the optional acoustic glazing, with tyre and wind noise well damped (64.6 dB(A) at 130 km/h).
Reviewer lists very good performance as a strength of the A6 Avant 2.0 TFSI e-hybrid quattro.
Reviewer criticises high electric consumption (26.8 kWh/100 km incl. charging losses), giving 83 km of measured electric range from the 20.7 kWh net battery versus 104 km WLTP.
Reviewer lists the lack of a DC fast-charging port as a weakness; the plug-in hybrid charges only by AC at up to 11 kW (about 150 minutes).

rationale: Audi's dedicated 800-V electric E-segment model on the PPE platform and the direct rival of the BMW i5 / i5 Touring; ADAC names the i5 Touring as its first competitor and AUTO ZEITUNG tests the A6 Avant e-tron quattro head to head against the i5 xDrive40 Touring.

statement: Reviewer rates the optional adaptive air suspension as among the best in the upper-midsize segment: very fine response in town and remarkably calm, luxury-class body control on country roads and motorways.
quote: zum Besten im Segment der oberen Mittelklasse

statement: Reviewer praises stoic straight-line stability, a rear that stays planted under braking or lift-off, a very safe ADAC evasion test and precise positioning near the limit despite almost 2.3 t.
quote: sehr gute Fahrstabilität und kurzer Bremsweg

statement: Reviewer states the steering feels somewhat decoupled and synthetic in Audi fashion and wishes for better feedback, though it is firmer and better defined than in the Q6 e-tron.
Reviewer states the 4.93 m length and a large 12.5 m turning circle make the car rather unwieldy, and rear-axle steering is not available.

Reviewer praises the predictive automatic recuperation using route data, limits and traffic ahead, an almost imperceptible blend into the friction brake and a 'B' mode for one-pedal driving even with a full battery; stopping distance is a good 32.8 m.
Reviewer states the 381 PS rear motor accelerates vehemently (0-100 km/h 5.4 s, 60-100 km/h 2.6 s) with smooth, well-modulated, almost vibration-free delivery.
Reviewer criticises that Auto Hold no longer has a separate button and must be activated awkwardly with a firm press on the brake pedal at every stop.
Reviewer states Ecotest consumption of 17.9 kWh/100 km incl. charging losses is remarkably low, below some small EVs, thanks to the heat pump and cd 0.24 aerodynamics, giving about 580 km of range.
Reviewer states the 800-V system charged 10-80 % in 23 minutes with a 283 kW peak and about 200 kW average, adding over 400 km, and two illuminated AC ports (one per side) add flexibility.
Reviewer criticises that battery preconditioning can only be triggered by entering a fast charger as a navigation destination; manual activation is not possible.
Reviewer finds the slow opening and closing of the electrically operated charging flaps somewhat annoying.
Reviewer praises the standard front trunk, which holds the charging cables without using boot space and stays reachable when the boot is loaded.

Reviewer states the boot (490 l, up to 1,460 l) is easy to use thanks to the power tailgate, a low 65 cm sill, a variable floor almost level with the sill and very good lighting; the 2.1 t towing capacity is large.
Reviewer states rear legroom is generous (knees touch only at 2.05 m with front seats set for 1.85 m) and headroom suits 1.95 m, with the optional panoramic roof giving a great sense of space.
Reviewer states the rear knee angle is rather sharp because of the EV-typical raised floor, and the standard front seats adjust only mechanically for height, fore-aft and backrest.

Reviewer states material quality falls well short of the outgoing A6 C8 and of a 100,000-euro premium car: cloth seats and inserts, soft plastic only on upper areas, scratch-prone hard plastic below, piano black instead of chrome, and felt instead of carpet in the boot.

Reviewer states the car also sounds less premium: the small compartment left of the wheel rattles when closed, doors close less solidly, touch fields click cheaply, and the plain plastic key feels much cheaper than before.

Reviewer calls the optional virtual exterior mirrors (1,450 EUR) impractical: each glance needs a refocus that tires the eyes on motorways, and missing depth makes distances and closing speeds hard to judge; a test drive is advised before ordering.
Reviewer states small windows, a high beltline, wide D-pillars and fixed rear headrests make all-round and rear visibility only adequate, so the driver relies on the standard rear camera and sensors.
Reviewer rates the Matrix LED headlights (Tech Plus package, 4,920 EUR) as very good, with a bright, even, wide beam and an optional headlight washer.

Reviewer states the quick-select fields for navigation, radio and menu on the left of the central display are hidden by the steering-wheel rim for most drivers, the quick menu needs an awkward swipe behind the wheel, and the fields are too small.
Reviewer praises the standard OLED panorama display for razor-sharp resolution, deep blacks and very good anti-glare, curved so the right edge stays reachable, with an intuitive menu structure.
Reviewer states climate control runs entirely through the central display without clear separation; functions cannot be felt, touch fields are small, and air distribution requires a submenu.
Reviewer states the feel-less touch keys on the steering wheel work jerkily and only conditionally reliably, turning interaction into frustration rather than pleasure.
quote: kein Genuss, sondern viel mehr Verdruss

statement: Reviewer criticises that the light controls are combined with mirror and central-locking keys in a touch panel in the driver's door that works as unreliably as the steering-wheel keys.

Reviewer states the instrument cluster offers neither a classic speedometer nor a large map view; the digital speed display's flanking scales are too coarse and small, so it distracts rather than being reliably readable.
Reviewer states voice control reliably handles frequently used operating steps.
Reviewer welcomes the physical cruise-control stalk, the rotary volume control in the console and info points that explain many settings.
Reviewer states the very large optional head-up display shows many active contents (highlighted lead vehicle, red distance bars) that carry some distraction potential.

Reviewer notes standard three-zone automatic climate with a separate rear control panel, vent wheels that set intensity independently of direction (also rear), and pre-conditioning via infotainment or app.

Reviewer states the optional lane-guidance assistant with adaptive cruise reliably relieves the driver on motorways, adopts speed limits automatically and rarely misreads them; a physical button on the indicator stalk toggles lane functions without looking.
Reviewer finds it surprising that Audi offers no automatic lane change on the A6 e-tron, nor (yet) a direct tyre-pressure monitoring system.
Reviewer reports a whirring from the front of the car around 100 km/h that attentive drivers may find annoying, as in the Q6 e-tron, although overall noise is low (65.4 dB(A) at 130 km/h).
Reviewer states the flush door handles with a touch area in the recess feel unusual at first but work better in practice than electrically retracting handles.
Reviewer notes the optional keyless system is configurable (e.g. unlock on approach) and measures key distance, so it cannot be opened via a relay attack.
Reviewer notes five Euro NCAP stars with 91 % for occupant protection and main assistance systems (emergency braking, lane keeping, adaptive cruise) as standard.
Reviewer criticises the package policy: many extras come only in large, partly very expensive packages, the test car reached 103,475 euros from a 77,250-euro base and still lacked leather.
Reviewer notes there are no grab handles on the headliner, which is impractical.
Reviewer ranks the A6 Avant e-tron quattro second with 3,292 of 5,000 points, narrowly behind the BMW i5 xDrive40 Touring (3,305).
Reviewer names the Audi the most efficient car in the test (21.2 vs 23.7 kWh/100 km for the i5 Touring) and the long-distance king with 448 km versus 343 km total range.
Reviewer states the Audi has to give way to the BMW in charging performance at the fast charger, despite its higher listed DC peak (270 vs 205 kW).
Reviewer praises the Audi's air suspension for comfort on all surfaces, while the BMW's air-sprung rear axle reacts more sensitively to edges and long undulations.
Reviewer states the Audi offers good road feel and grip, but the i5 Touring has more mechanical grip and is more agile at the limit.
Reviewer states the BMW pulls away from the more powerful Audi in acceleration and top speed (0-100 km/h 5.2 vs 5.4 s; 215 vs 210 km/h).
Reviewer states the Audi has the highest share of hard plastic in the test and a less rigid body than its rivals.
Reviewer states the Audi's sport seats suit long distances but are less adjustable than the BMW's comfort seats.
Reviewer states the Audi's high rear floor forces an unnatural sitting posture in the back, while the BMW's rear seat angle is more comfortable.
Reviewer notes the Audi has a practical front storage compartment that the BMW lacks.
Reviewer rates the Audi's load area as less usable than the BMW's (502-1,422 l vs 570-1,700 l).
Reviewer names the BMW the quietest car in the test; the Audi is louder at 50 km/h (61 vs 58 dB(A)) and level at 100/130 km/h.
Reviewer states the Audi has the higher base price (81,450 vs 77,600 EUR) and calls the BMW the cheapest at the checkout, though the Audi's extra cost is limited.
Reviewer states the Audi has the lowest running costs, the best depreciation and the best insurance classification in the test.
Long-term tester states the charger-finding tools in both Android Auto and the car's own system worked well, showing charger speed and free plugs during a trip to France.
Long-term tester reports rapid charging gained about 150 miles in a 20-minute stop and found French rapid chargers with bank-card payment almost seamless.
Long-term tester reports 3.2 mi/kWh overall, matching the official 4.0 mi/kWh only in slow 50 mph traffic, and at 80 mph range fell from about 350 to about 260 miles (WLTP 443 miles).
Long-term tester found the car composed and comfortable on motorways, with a smooth ride and stable tracking, though composed rather than fun.
Long-term tester found the boot very large for a family of four on holiday.
Long-term tester states the parcel shelf must be detached before loading a full boot, to avoid bending it when closing the tailgate.
Long-term tester states rear legroom is limited because the bench sits low, forcing taller passengers to bend their knees, and under-thigh support could be better.
Long-term tester states the voice control did not understand his commands.
Long-term tester reports the touch-to-open charging flaps kept opening while the car was being washed.
Long-term tester praises the Malpelo Blue paint and the estate's shape.
Long-term tester finds the EV-specific front, with blanked grille and a body-coloured panel between the headlights, less appealing than the petrol/hybrid A6.
Long-term tester states the black plastic sill panels look cheap and pick up fingerprints.
Owner (A6 Avant e-tron quattro, experienced BEV driver) reports real motorway range above 450 km, doing two non-stop 404 km legs mostly at about 150 km/h on about 22.4 kWh/100 km.
Owner reports charging 54.9 kWh from 9 % to 63 % in 13 minutes at an IONITY charger, briefly seeing 280 kW, with a charging curve better than expected.
Owner rates the driver assistance as the best on the market: adaptive cruise, lane keeping and sign-based speed adaptation work well, with timely braking for limits and smooth acceleration.
Owner names the missing overtaking (automatic lane-change) assistant as the only limitation of the assistance system.
Owner finds the sign-based speed control often too slow for their taste.
Same owner reports over 340 km of range in winter below -5 degrees C at average speeds above 120 km/h.

statement: Forum user who drove an A6 e-tron (not owned) enjoyed it and considers Audi's assistance systems a current reference, worth paying extra for on the motorway.
Forum user who drove two A6 e-tron workshop loan cars says Audi is no longer premium except in its prices.
